Well, I never before, saw as much, or heard so I much ,of that gray-headed old worthy • Santa Claus.' It almost seems as if Europeans, and their descend- ants, the further they get away from fatherland, cling more tenaciously and seek to instil more life into the traditions of their forefathers, and the joys of their childhood. We all remember, as the years golmund, the pleasure of taking the youngsters •• up street earls returning Christmas-tide, and the shouts of pleasure, and the tuggings made by each earnest son and daughter of Santa Claus, to get a closer view of the toys displayed in the slsop win- dows. It is not always a pleasant sight one meets, , when strolling through the streets at Christmas. r To see no many wistful eyes turned longingly, yet 1 in vain, towanle the beautiful toys, often causes a! sharp pang in the breast of the would-beplsilan-1 thropist. And yet when we come right down to it, at what a small cost is real downright pleasure given at home, when the family, big children as well as little children, gather round the presents Santa Claus has been good enough to bestow. No one perambulating San Francisco could fancy : furs moment that anything but plenty would crown the board this festive season. Christmas Day itself w-as wretched ; a wearisome drizzle struggled with a muggy fog for mastery. All the same, swarms of men and women crowded the streets from morn till night. All the kuling stores are so arranged that customers find with the great- est ease the various counters at which their wants are likely to he supplied. And. ols what parcels are earried,and wheeled, or trundled out of these stores. Dolls! Never before slid I see such beautiful speci- mens of the doll maker's craft. None need turn away. From the child of the poorest, to the child of the richest millionaire, all can be supplied. The amateur housekeeper only just beginning to toddle, may find displayed a beautiful kitchen fitted up with every necessary, sisal, tired of cooking, may toddle into the bedroom, where all is again complete Donkeys and ponies to suit equestrians of all ages are fixed up its the windows, gazing stolidly at the flattened noses which are pressed against the immense plate-glass windows. Oh. but this is the children's paradise. I never before saw anything to compare with it. Almost every man and woman one meets in the street is literally loaded with the results of Santa Claus' prompting,

I must ask our Editor to look a little leniently en our little failings, and be to our , little faults a little blind. tiers am! in California a State which is depending largely on its wine production, and sh.tild I not encourage the staple industry 'of the country? Of course :so here's to my friends at home in a bumper of California wine: . . .

/To be motione(.)

bills nttoat Christmas time,- -good drinking, or ' excessive eating it I know I have several strong abstaining readers—not from eating, but drinking .--and I put this to them al a conundrum. We have some tolerably good peckers here ; I read of one as boasting in thislvay . " A toastol dank an appetizer caddie; Followed by ten enormous salmon trout; And with each fish I put my friends to shame By swallowing a tun of Dublin stout." Of course,we don't have toasted sharks every day. Just previous to sitting down to ray desk, had been in the city with one, who, all being well, will lend to the alter my eldest daughter on New Year's Day. That is to say, the par,on is duning down to my house during tile oft,enoon ot that day- there to tie the knot, Sc.. A;c. Well ; we had keen in Ike city to make provision for the inward man. The result is that a turkey weighing 271bs. will grace the head of the table ; of course after your humble servant. Well, Christmas will be over with you. my good readerdong ere this epistle readies you. In &not her few days it will be over with no. and down again we must settle to sober work and the responsibilitieu of life. It seems but a short time since "me and mine" left the good old town, and yet what changes have come about. Death has been busy, and I notice, as I scan my "Examiner," that new navies are already beginning to appe,arand take their place in your township's matters. its the world goes on. Wears always making way for others to follow. 13 Valparaiso-st., San Francisco. Dec. '2Bth, 1888.

Helens Town Hall, on Thursday afternoon, Mr. Brighouse held as inquest I m the body of Patrick Wynne. aged thirty years, who was killed in the Havannah Colliery% belonging to Messrs. It. Evans and Ce., on Tuesday. Mr. Ball, Government inspector of mines, occupied a seat on the bench with the coroner. Decease,l was working at a face twelve or fourteen yards wide when a fall :of top coal and roof took place, and Wynne shouted • " Tom, help me out." A miner named Connor took his hand, but mom roof fell, and the latter ran off, and only just escaped, as the coal caught his heels. Wynne died unmediately I, was got out. div.p: LORD DERRY OP EMIGRATION.

..„ .... ... -..-... Lord Derby addressed the fret anima/ meeting of the Liverpool Self.llelp Emigration Society On Monday. The noble Earl mid that for a nation situated as ours, an out- fit,. of population WWI an absolute necessity; and for this overnow emigration, though not an adequate remedy, was at Wiwi a palliative. The chief difficulty of the emigration untedson was the danger of exciting ottonialjealousy by sending too many competitors for Pmployment. The idea of settling people on unoccupied lends at home was not excluded by the emigration vvatern ; bet if • man could get a hundred acres in esnada for leas than he would have to pay for ton acre, in this country, Isis Lordship thought be had better move.

div.head: REV. C. A. BERRY AT WARRING-
div.p: THE REV. C. A. BERRY AT WARRING-
TON.

IThe Rev. C. A. Berry, of Wolverhampton, who declined the offer of the congregation of the Ply- mouth Church, Brooklyn, to succeed the late Rev. Henry Ward Beecher as pastor there, occepied the pulpit at Wycliffe Congregational Church, Warring- ton, on Sunday. Mr. Berry's fame as a preacher drew together large congregations, and the Church was crowded both at the morning and even* services. Collections were made in aid of the Lancashire Congregational Union and Church Aid Society. At the evening service the rev. gentleman took as his text the words Then said one unto hint, Lord, are there few that he saved?" And he said unto them, Strive to enter in at the strait gate, for many, I nay unto you, will seek to enter in and shall not be able "—Lake xiii. 23-24. It was, he said, painfully clear to the least thoughtful amongst them that the tendency of ordinary life was towards a dull and unimpassioned routine of thought and feeling, blind to the shoreims infinite which stretched beneath their feet, and dead to the timeleas eternal that eehoed back their heart throbs. It win one of the penalties one of the curses, of our artificial civilisation, that we were so increasingly absorbed in the whirl of clamorous engagements that we had little time, and less rapacity, for the vivid inqtressions, the heroie thoughts, the simple and stirring motives of ages richer yet earlier than our own. In his essay on John Milton, Lord Macaulay said that as civilis- ation advanced poetry almost necessarily declined. It was but an adaptation of that literary judgment to say that . our life shaped itself into systems of thought habits of emotion, and routines of action, there wait a tendency to the less of wonder, reverence, and inspir- ation, and there was a risk of it becoming a nice' soul- less mechauism. It was when thoughts nude as these laid hold of him that he turned with gratitude to the . Christian Sabbath and the Christian sanctuary. There, at least, they had breathing time amid life's eager activ. j ities. There, if only for an hour, the call u-ax sounded and the opportunity was given to riot to higher things, I in stillness, and meditation, Imi prayer. There I were always plenty of people in the world who seemed to have been twisted into notesof interroga- tion. They were the people who "want to know you know," and they would break most unbitnliingly into the most serious discourses with miserable little ques- tions and foolish inquiries, always irrevelant and often impertinent. Sometimes the disciples fell into that pry- ing curiosity, and, amid the solemnities that character- ised the Last Supper they disregarded Christ's agony and bloody sweat to ask questions. Questions as to what? As to which of them should be grttattxt. Some- times those quesiioners were neither fnend nor foe, but a familiar acquaintance known to us all, the social I nuisance pure and simple, the simple gossip, the man with the note hook and the ever sharpened pencil, and the man who wascollecting what he was pleased to call inbtresting facts. Oh, what a inisery were these curious questioners, who lived on not. of interrogation. It must have been a man of this stamp who asked the question in the text. It woo the question of a man who had grown up in a narrow, mechanical, exclusive school of thought. Them was a good reason why the question should not be answered. Statistics were always more or less mischievous. Statistics of the future, projected by prophesy on to the arena of the present, would surely be thnce mischievous. Christ would answer no such question as that. He would tell them that tiotEs grace woo free and would give them the message that thensues of the future depended upon the activities of the present. His answer, if they looked wisely at it, ara.s equivalent to this—. Mind your own bosiness, and leave to litsl and to Divine secrecy the things which Concern hhi eternal purpose. Don't meddle with matters you can't under- stand. Do this rather--see after yourself and your own position. Get you inside thegate, and then there will be at least one saved, and one added to the number, be it great or small." That did not mean that every man should look after himself and leave others lode the same, but was directed against prtang hit° the seen.. of God. It meant that a man had" better stop talking, and questiaming, and istplexing himself and others as to the number of the savedand pay some attention to the practical matter of his man rcdeniption ; that it were wiser to leave to God what belonged to Hint It was a rebuke which should serve for the guidance of them all. 111 modern christemlien he was conscious of two classes of supposed religionists. First, there were the men who had no particular interests and who asked no questions. 'rhey were solleitons enough about their business, health, and comfort, and they studied every morningthe prices teltegraphed from the Exchange. I They would ask many questions as to what would snimster to the comfort of the body, and of their sur - roundings. Standing on the point of tent,' we called to- day, which was in itself an impenetrable mystery, breathing the breath of Gars life, feeling, if thee felt at all, the pulsations of a great mysterious eutiSciollaneMi within themselves, they asked no questions ! They had no interest ; they were Lauren ; they were dead. There was another class—the men who never did anything except ask questions. They would ask the meaning ot them, the explanation of that, not because they were yearning to increose their information, not because they were solivitous to have a new base on which to Wilda life of Christian activity, but only just to gratify a passing interest. There were also people by hundreds lathe Christian churches of England who said that they would never submit themselves to the claims of religion until everything was made kii,Ml to them— clear as the sun at noontide. Suppose a man should tell them that he would not travel by railway until he had mastered the philosophy of steam and machinery, or that he would not vat bread until he had mastered all the chemistry of food. They had abetter philosophy for daily life. He (Mr. Berry) had learn studying theology for many years, and Its had reached tlustmant—he never knew so little about it as he did to-day, and that waS true id' every earrext student. The more a man studied, and the more Ile learned, the further he felt himself from the great goal, but this lee did know, that Christ was good,that His word was true, and that the God who made him did sot do sate mock hint, but to save and bless him. There was a strait gate to the Kingdom if wealth, and to the Kingdom of knowledge, and men strive to enter in. The strait gate to the Kingdom of Ilttaven was open, and he exhorted them to strive to enter. They windd then stop I asking questions about the number of the elect, and . would know that the God who had been able tosavethem . was StrollgenooKh, deep enouglband fabreaching enough j to save all who came to Him.

LABOUR ELECTORAL ASSOCIATION. A BRANCH AT WARRINGTON.

On Saturday evening a meeting of workmen engaged in various trades in Warrington was held in the Ragged School, Betray-st., "to consider the question of forming a branch of the labour Electoral Association in Warrington." Mr. S. Donbobbin was elected to the chair, and he was supported on the platform by Councillor Threlfall, of Southport. The CHAIRMAN said that Mr. Threlfall would propound to them a scheme which would probably be beneficial to the working eifISSeR. They all knew that they were represented in Parliament by men who did not think much of their affairs nor yet cared much for their benefit. Ile might refer to the syndicates dim were now in operation in the country and to others that were about to be formed to monopolise the supply of things that were necessary to the comfort of the people. (Hear, hear.) All i this went to show that t was necessary that work- ing people should combine to send representatives to the House of Commons, and to their local Parlia- ments as well, from amongst themselves. (Ap- plause.) Councillor THRELFALL said he was glad to find that Warrington was one of the few towns in Lancashire which had, up to the present, been sufficiently alive to the fact that its interests in the Town Council could not be better looked after than by a workingman. It was, therefore, a matter of sincere pleasure to him to see the return of Mr. Councillor Flood at the last November election. (Ilear, hear.) He hoped they would go on in the same course and return a number of other work- ingmen to the Town Council. (Hear. hear.) They might be asked if they were not satisfied with the present system of representation Ann workingman he said, "No." and there ware thousands more of workingmen who would say the salmi. They imuld not be mtislied with a system of representation which put into the HOUSC Of Commons 209 landowners, 139 lawyers, 62 railway directors, 20 ironniasters,22 shipowners, and above 100 manufacturers and m erchants. These men represented interests which wen. often diametrically opposed to the interests of working people, interests which workmen were continu- ally striking and struggling against. If it was for the benefit of these men to get into the House of Commons to represent their interims, it was still more important that the ism-rest and must cancerous class throughout the kingdom should send thor men to the Heise of Ciannions to represent their intercate. (Applause.) The since had come when labour must strike for itself, must emancipate itself. It was of no good saying ” Trust the chimes ” He who would be free,hiniself must strike the blow.” (Applause.) If there had been fifty workmenin the House of Commons during the pact 50 years the position of the working classes would have been superior to what it is to-day ; there would have been some tendency at least towards the more equitable dim tribution of the profits and results of labour. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Threlfall then proceeded to explain objects of the work of the Electoral Association. In Yorkshire, in the neighbourhood of Bradford and Ilingley, there were numerals branches of the Association and they abounded pretty extensively in Nottinghamshire. It was desired to create a lawful and powerfu organisation amongst them —to so organise that instead of their having to go to the political parties the political parties would come cap in hand to the m. The Association was formed two years age by the Trades Unimista of the kingdom who thought it was necessary to float such an orgmimtion in order that all sections of labour might combine together and go powerfully for- ward, and the results had exceeded all their anticic- bons. The local association.s, he explained, were but fastened down to any system ; they were given ho The rule no that they could manage their own affairs in their own was. All that was asked of them was to unite with : others to help forward the general movement. They could take any action an a branch in their partieular town. They could run half-a-dmen !Abair candidatm ! for the Town Council if they liked, and if the central authority could help them it would, and if they wanted ! a candidate for the House of Commons it would do all it possibly could not only in regard to speakers but also (flear, hear.) With regard to the pro- gramme of the Association he enumerated the following points i—Payment of members of the Mime of Commons: payment id returning officer's expenms ; taxation of ground rents ; nationalieation of theland; adultsuffrage and reform of gni registration laws ; free education ; national Parliaments for England, Scotland, and Wales, with an Imperial Parliament for the joint affairs of the whole ) dime. tablishment and &endowment stall State churches ; reform or the poor law : eight hours bill for miners and reduction of Si,,, hours of labour in all employ- ments rimfiring Parliamentary sanctien and in Govern. meat works ; triennial Parliaments ; nationalisation of royalty Cola; abolition of sinecure offices and the establishinent of hoards of conciliation betwoen employers and emploveC.s. Toms's the close of his speech Mr. Threlfall ilia forcible and eloquent manner urged upon those present the necessity of combination amongst workingmen fur the purpose of returning suitable repro- eentatives. (Applause.) Mr. .1. Cl/overnice thought that some of the questions that had been brought before them would want further !consideration, but he had pleasure in mewing the follow- ing resolution That this meeting nf workingmen, , ! representing all branches of labour in Warrington, is of ! : opinion that the Labour Electoral Association is a step is, the right direction for making better the condition of the • : mns of toil and hereby rmolvas to become a branch of

.... . I Mr. E. Wftiony seconded the proposition, which was supported by M. E. Jukes and several others, arid carried unanimously. ALLEGED FRAUD ON A WARRINGTON TRADESMAN.

Yesterday morning, at the Borough Police Court, a married woman named Martha Carley was brought up in custody on a charge of having, on the 26th November last, she being the bailee of a piano, the property of Messrs. G. and J. Weaver. converted the same to her own use, and thereby stolen it. Mr. A. Browne, who appeared for the prosecution, stated that on the :24th of November last the prisoner called at the shop of Messrs. G. and J. Weaver, Bridge-st., and selected a piano, value £2l, which was delivered on the following day. An agreement was entered into in the name of the defendant herself, by which she was to become the hirer of the piano, and pay Li a month , until the .1:25 had been paid and it became her pro- perty. She was bound not to sell the piano, or I remove it from her address, without having pre- vious consent in writing. She paid .Cl, and when the second instalment was due she ask.' Mr. Weaver to let her off paying it, and she would pay .ClO in January, when she expected to receive some money. This was agreed to, but sub- sequently Mr. Weaver found that prisoner and her husband had left home, and that everything had been sold up. It was afterwards ascertained that the piano in question had been pawned for ten guinea., the prisoner having made a declaration to the effect that she was the absolute owner of it. A warrant was issued and she was apprehended near Glasgow. Mr. Browne said that there were creditors of the prisoner in the town to the amount of about .010. and he understood that there was another charge in regard to a piano. Prisoner, when apprehended, had .£l6 in her possession, and he applied that that should not be given up at present. lie also asked for a remand, The case was then remanded until Tuesday next.

The publishers of one of the leading society papers of London have taken to analysing some of the I leading patent medicines. also to investigating !their published testimonial,, with the result of creating quite a commotion among certain proprie- tors. Injurious effects likely to follow the use of patent medicines, published testimonials given from addresses which only exist in the mind of a clever writer in the company's employ, are fully exposed. Suits for heavy damages have been threatened by the proprietors of the remedies thus exposed. Injured innocence puts on a bold front, but the publishers of the paper in question do not frighten easily •, they have taken spa question of vital interest to the public, and they pop.ae to turn on the full light of intelligent investigation. One meet excellent feature of this exposure is, that the public are enabled to discriminate between worthless nostrums and those nastily good remedies. The publishers evidently take this view of the .questiom for their last investiga- tion is a most flattenng one for the proprietor, of that noted remedy St. Jacobs oil. EXAMINER,
SATURDAY. JANUARY 26. 1883.

IMr. Jim,: NIORLEVS speech at Sheffield, iii Monday, was .sie of the longest and strongest he has yet made. It toadies a wide range of topics, awl it illuminates everything that it toadies. The " Ties' has tried to write Mr. MORLEY down as " a la sikish theorist," but epithets don't stick to a man unless they are appropriate. In this case the epithet dots; not lit, for, although the member for Newcastle is. book man of the first rank, he is wit at all "bookish." Let a reader test this by plunging into one of his spemilms at any point he will instantly perceive that there is no fine- spun argument; that, on the ixintrary, the issue, whatever it may be, is stated with andoubtial skill and grace but at the same time with homeliness and direetnesa Besides, we Imre it on good authority that 110 man was ever writtou down, except by himself, and the axiom is one which applies to speakers as well as writers. Mr. 3.101t1.M1( wrote himself up to the rank of Cabinet Minister, and it is not at all an unlikely supposition that he will speak himself up to be Prime Minister of England. He is a theorist, of course, in the sense that all thoughtful men are theorists. He was ono of the first aneiitgst Liberals of standing to perceive that Coercion in Ireland stood in the way of the success of every reform ; and that the right treatment of the sister ink was to leave the ! Irish to manage their own affairs in their OWII way. , Galileo was a theorist when lie net forth the pro- • position that the earth was round, and that it moved in space. Ile was pat in gaol for prolamin!- , ing a theory which was then regarded as monstrous and heretical ; but mankind have long since come to the conclusion that Galileo was right- —just as mankind are beginning to think that Mn Morley is right in having faith in Conciliation as opposed to Coercion. He has not been put in prison, for he is im Englishman ; but if lie laid been what he is, with the sole differenim of being an Irish instead of an English member of Parliament, he would have been in gust years ago.

The late Mr. PETER RYLANUN once said that if he had been an Irishman hoshould have been a rebel ; and the conduct of the Government in the :irdministration of the Crimes Act is such that it is patriotism on the part of Irishmen to rebel. There is a stage in despotism at which "rebellion against tyranny becomes obedience to God ; and it is long since that stage was matched in Ireland. But it does not follow from this that Irishmen would be justified in taking rifles in their hands, and ' raising civil war. A revolution of this kind can only be justified when another means have failed, and when there is a reasonable prospect of over- cawing the tyrants of the hour. All other means have not failed; the Appeal to the people of Wales and of Scotland has succeded ; and signs are not , lacking that, at the next election, it will be found to have macc,aled in England. Meantime the duty of Irish leaders is to ad, as they are doing, according to conscience, when they find that coercion will lult permit them to obey the law. The other day Mr. E. HARRINGTON, M.P., was brought before a Resident Magistrate for publishing, in his own newspaper, a report of a speech winch was made at a meeting of a "nap. pressed" branch of the National League. He believed it ti be his duty to publish that report just as we should feel it our duty to report a political meeting in this country, whatever might be the folly of the law. In the couriu: a the trial, Mr. HARKIN OTON WUB asked if he would " promise not to naieat the offence, not to publish any more of these reports." If he had made the required promise, he would have been net at liberty; but he was not to be intimidated. He , set the law at defiante. We put it to every reader ; —Tory, Unionist, or Liberal, whom these lines ' may reach—Was Mr. HARUINOTON not in the right in refusing to make the promise Would he not have been a coward, and a traitor to Ins conscienos, if, to escape I hment, he had turned aside from doing what he believed to be his: duty ? And what was the punishment for following the onlionry eiiiir..te of a newspaper proprietor ? Sir mad& aith hard labour, and he is under- I going that "savage, vindictive, alai feri.ions sentence" at this toonient. We find it difficult to write eisilly about such an infamy---for infamy it is when it is recollected that prosecutions of Ws kind have been abandoned for twelve mouths, and that other papers TORUIRI untouched altlffingli they reported the same meeting. We leave it ' rather to Mr. Moni.er to utter conilonination in aiim Date terms. lt,ferring to this matter he said aw _

-•••••- Gentlemen, I have been responsible for the government if Ireland- and so I may be again. I Loud ele.ers.) With all that in my mind, I say • deliberately that the sentence passed under those circumstances was a disgrace to the magistrate who passed i, and was a disgrace to the Parliament and the Government who gave such power to the magistrate yes, and it is a d6grace to you the , workingmen of Sheffield who send three gentlemen to Parnament to support that system. (Load cheers.)

Tho diswace, let us add, attaches to its all, mid it is a diem:tee which grows wider and deeper every day that the present Government remain in office. They are excessively bridal, and insufferably mean: 111110 day a newspaper proprietor is given six months hard labour for reporting a meeting ; another day a presiman is sent to gaol because he declines to IN,COIIIO a common informer; people arc 114011011 11111 bayoneted when they assemble to welcome one of their leaches ; and we have a member of Pain mt arrested because. he has made himself offensive by assisting, at

" Sweet See the ii,,,. if adversity.- Lord SALISBURY sought to degrade that distingnished • Indian gentleman Mr. DADARIIAI Nsinion by referring to him as "a black man." The insult was no keenly felt and so strongly resented by the natives of India that there has been a reaction which has re,alted in the degradation of the Prime Ministiv. It is it matter of amazement hi outsiders that a Prime Minister could have said aanything indiscreet- -not to say offensive: but it is Lord SALIsSURY'S way, and the nation had a W'°°°"° siws•inien of his insolence when he COM- peril the li••!,,•!, of Ireland hi Hottentots. It was hard lel Mr. N.ionon that he shonld be singled out Liii OIVIW tele, beelelSe he sought to represent hi:: ciellithymen in the Bimini if Commons: len he is delightfully avenged. Ile, owes it to the sneer that, on Monday evening, the I largest complimenthry dinner was given to him that has yet I oisin held in the Natimed Libera ChM. Lord Biros, pmiiiled, and this Wlan iiiclose priate in an espixial degree, for his lordship is held in affectionate remembrance by the natives of India as the Vihuroy who, above all others, let ill be seen of all men that he was there ti carry out the great Liberal principle 14 "trust in the people." His speech as chairman was marked, like his speeches, with good sense and good taste. Lord SALISBURY was " let Mr easily no far as direct allusion to his offence went; but it was none the less a weighty rebuke to point out that Mr. NACIROa ARA a gentleman of whom Indians IRA Englishmen might be proud, seeing that he bad won his way from the teaching stair of a great college tin the hearts of his countrymen, !and to the high position of Primo Minister of the State Id Ranala. The death, on Monday, of the Bishop of St. Asaph, has called forcible attention to what is a scandal in the Church. and that is that the clergy sometimes cling to the loaves and hell.a when they are long past rendering tit service for them. The aged Bishop of St. Asaph was incapable for sonic thou before his death 14 even either resigning or making appointments. There can be no harm, when " veterans lag superfluous MI the stage," in their being asked to retire. There is always a I/01MM for them. Fancy a collier, or an editor, living allowed to draw his full wages when no longer capable of doing his work.

Speaking at the meeting of the Liverpool Inks:sem Benefices Augmentation Fund, on Mon- day, the Bishop of Liverpool said " livnago seemed ;to be decreasing in value. The public had no idea of the amount of expenses to be met by a clergy- man whose stipend was put at Cl,OOO a year. That meant no more than alsmt 4:700 after the • various rates and taxes were paid." It is very and, no doubt, from the point of view of a Bishop, to I think of the " living " of a follower s.f" the meek mid lowly" being reduced to e7OO a year. There are ordinary mortals, In mover, who woultlnt send trying to keep body and soul together with " no more than I:700" a year.

In this way be made bad worse. The breach, though small at first, 'on opening wide, In rushes Folly with a tun-moon tide.

In India there are 2:io millions of people ; and it is a monstrous doctrine that they are not to have as much as no representative in the House of Commons. The right policy is to strengthen Parliament by the admission of men who know something of the pressing wants of a people who were advanced in civilisation when the British ancestors of Loin. SMIRK-RR were painted and half-naked savages. They do not ask for Home • Rule as yet; but they do demand, and have a right to demand, that they shall have some voice in the Government of their (sundry. The County Council of Lancashire held its first meeting on Thursday, and decided as to the election of its 3.1 Aldermen that they should be chosen from the elected Councillors. At the first meeting of the Oxfordshire Conncil, Mr. Ritchie, and Mr. Walter Long—both members of the Government—were quoted as expressing the opinion that nit was the intention of Parliament that the Aldermen should be taken outside and not inside the County Council." Rut these gentlemen know, or ought to know, that " firms- diet contd. The Act gives power —just as in the eitNl3 of Town Councils --to elect Alder- men either from the inside or the outside; and each Council has a perfect right to please itself in the matter. The Aldermanic feature is a Ice! feature; hut if Aldermen are chosen from inside the Council it cannot, at any rate, be said that they have not in the first instants, run the gaunt- let of a ratepayers' election.

RUNCORN MUSICAL. SOCIETI"S CONCERT.

Tire lint concert in connection with the Ituncorn Musical Society. was given in Runcorn Public Hall, on Tuesday evening. Although the audience VMS not of dimensions such as might have been ex- , riveted, it was still f encouraging proportions. , The re-creed chairs were 11111 to overflowing : the I other seats being fairly well patronized; and it must be at once conceded that the concert was a distinct vitreous. It said much for the inditstry of the members, awl the ability of the conductor,that, within three months of its formation, the Society was able to place so admirable it programme before the public, and it is to be hoped that before the winter season gives place to Summer, another concert equally enjoyable will be arranged. The principals were Miss Lizzie Owen,Miss Annie Hope, Mr. r:. 11. Williarna (Runcorn), and Mr. David Eldwarls ; solo violin. Mr. Martin Hertz. The first part of ;he programme consistol of excepts from the sacred music of Handel, Nlendelssolin, Beet- hoven Haydn Ste., and commenced with this chorus. . . .

" 0 Father, wbos;'alinighty power," in who-h the choir of 70 voices gave pleasing is of the treat in store. The second part of the programme was filled with items of a miseellanoms character. Dealing first with the work of the chorus, let it be at the outset stated thattheir performances were tuneful, powerful, and well sustained througlmut, and were highly enjoyed. " The Heavens are telling," front Hardn's Creation, in which the sots, were ad ' ably taken by Miss Owen, Mr. Williams and Mr. Edwards, was very effectively ren- dered ; and the " Bridal chorus "woo a charming disc play of (art singing. The audience were not stinting of applause a, any part of the evening,but they evince.' enthusiastic appreciation of the singing of the part song " The Vikings," and the choir hail to repeat the two last verses. Of the principals, Miss Owen possesses a sweet, pure, soprano voice, and, aided by a clear eaunciation, she won the hearts if those present at the outset by an expressive rendering of Gounod's delightful Snag " There is a green hill." In the aria "Oh Robert, my beloved " (Robert the Devil) she dis- played a richness of tone, and a dramatic power of expression that called forth a tremendous ovation; but on Mr. Humphreys explaining that the lady was suffering from serious indisoccition, she was excused W,waiding to the earon, Possessed of p. nverful con- tralto voice, of extellent quality, Miss Hope is besidts a vocalist of ability, and for a capital rendering of "Creation's Hymn " she was recalled, and bowed her acknowledgments. A similar compliment was paid to her fiff her artistic interpretation of " In the Chimney f'onier," and she responded with "My true love, Jem." Miss Hope also sang " Punchinello " with appropriate exprassion of feeling. Mr. Edwards sang, " Ann, arm, ye brave " (Judas Maccabeus) by desire ; and " Oh, how the winds blow," besides taking part in several concerted pieces He displayed the true instincts of an artist and his vocalisation gave great satisfaction. He rereived a well merited encore for his descriptive rendering of the last tome.] song. Our lival vocalist, Mr. Williams, was ! an unqualified success. A tenor with a light voice of pure quality, which he tors to the best advantage, Mr. Williams gave a fine expositioe of the nvit and aria" If ! with all your hearts," and in response to an enthusiastic , encore, sung" Beautiful Annabel Lea." He wal actually suecessful in the aria" Where'er vim walk,' his render- ling being distinguished by remarkable taste and °sires- , rims. TYPICAL CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY. A conference in connection with the Cheshire and North Wales Co-operative Conference Associa- tion, was held at Gersten, on Saturday, when there I wore nearly fifty delegates present, including representatives from Warrington, St. Helens, and Runcorn. Mr. Thomas Birchen, who has for twenty- one years been president of the {Warrington Co- operative Society, read a paper on "A Typical Co-operative Society ; its difficulties and successes," which was listened to with the greatest interest. Mr. BIRCHALL said that the little history he WU about to relate was a simple record of the earnest work of a few hard-handed Lancashire men, who , achieved success because their faithfulness deserved it. About thirty years ago the minds of the people in this country, and more especially the minds ef the operatives in the northern counties, were greatly excited by the published results of an experiment that had been made by a number of Rochdale weavers, who, feeling the pressure of low wages and uncongenial surroundings, had had the auda- city to believe that they, wits their small means, and without previous commercial training, could inaugurate and carry on successfully, an under- taking that would kelp, both physically and mentally, to raise them in the social scale. Amongst the places where the results of the Rockdale experiments were eagerly din- reseed was Warrington, which, notwithstand- ing its conservative tendencies, had already made one or two small, but abortive, attempts in the same direction. A few enthusiastic young men realously I took the matter up, and a determination was come to that as soon ass capital of £lOO ...old be raised they would commence operations. Tie. desired amount seas got together, a committee and secretary appointed and a shop secured. For sonic time most of the business was ' transacted on the evenings of Tuesdays and Saturdays. and without any very startling experiences the move- ment jogged along through the first year, 1861. At the I close It was found that the sates amounted to about £llO tier week, and a dividend of is. 13.1. in the £ was , declared. The object of the society thus started was to improve the social and domestic condition of its mem- bers, by proving a safe and profitable investment for the savings of working-men, by combining the facilities of banking with the profits of "trade, by laying down ready-money trade as an unalterable basis, by providing means for social intercourse and improving the intellec- tual and moral omdition of its members, by fostering business habits and encouraging thrift, and by affording a field for the earrying out of beneficial reforms such AS open and fair dealing, early closing, he. It was not without special effort that they managed to keep a firm adherence to some of these principles. At the- end id the fifth quarter the discovery was made that the profits had fallen to at least ono-half of what they had previously been, although the sales had Ixs-n pro- gressive, and, although rigid inquiry was made, it was not easy to and the leakage. A few individuals began to indulge in carping criticism, disloyalty to the legally appointed offirers of the Society, and a disregard of its real interests followed, and, as the Committee were not working harmoniously, changes were made in that direction. But the downward course had been started. and it could not be quickly stopped by a recon- strurted committee. At the end of the sixth quarter it was found that the profits hail vanished altogether, and that there could bone dividend. The writer of hie paper, then a working wire-drawer, had just been appointed president, and only those who had been similarly situated could estimate the worry and anxiety which all concerned in the management had had to pass through. Friends who had stood by them when things went smoothly now deserted, the sales, which had reached some £l4O per week,tell to about one-third of that AUM' and bed it not been furs faithful few who did not know WIICII they were beaten the history of the Society would have been a short and a melancholy one. A rigid examination VIM instituted, no stone was left unturned in the effort to ensure success, and gradually, though it was uphill work, they hegan to make I progress. slinager after manager was tried, and resigned, until a young workman who had served on the tommittee,and had always stood firmly by , Co-operative principles, undertook the position at the munificent salary of 260. per week. Ile worked harmoniously for the Committee, gained increased respect, and, though he had never asked ferns advance., had for the past five years received a well earned salary of £3OO a year. A career of steady progress had now been entered upon, and the present prioniscs, at a tntbled mitt. were taken. Some years later they purchased the whole bloek of five buildings on a yearly ground rent, and, a building fund having been accumulated, "fullest don-n and rebuilt three suitable shops and a CIIIIIMOdiOIIS, hall at a cost of £5,000. Though this wxsmore than eleven yl'af, IWO that sum had been nearly cleared off, along with some £2,000, :Mgt of plant and fixtures which had been entirely cleared off by depreciation. They were now building in another part of ela town a handsome suite of shops, warehouses "and bakery, as the ws-sent premises were completely ginned with business. For the 25 years they had steadily incrensed their dividend.s, had never receded one penny, and hadsteadily lessened their liahilitits. They bad Hot aimed at paying large dividends, but so successful had their system been that they could not now help paying them. Their dividend for two years had been 3s. 2d. in the £, and the reserve fund, which amounted toabout £l,BOO n year, WWI being increased at the rite of £3OO a year. Tfiere was also an educational fund amounting ti nearly £4OO, for the giving of free lectures and the support of the news-room. Last year, at a reasonable estimate, the society's nssets were worth fifty per cent. over ilO liabilitits. Mr. Itimhall then statest various courses of action that had largely contributed to this phenomenal success, which might also contribute he the success of othersometies. Briefly put, headvised careful- ness in the selection of einployeenestensive depreciation, and effectual auditing. They must not grab at big divid- ends, and must make their position safe by lessening liabilities, and honestly estimating goods in stock. The whole of the disposable profits should never be paid in dividends, but gond balances should be left to secure a continuity of divulend. These, with other means, he laid down as the result of his twenty-eight years' exper- ience and observation as an active worker in a society whose solid 5a1.C.48, he believed, was unsurpassed in , the Cixoperative movement. lie was hopeful that in the near future their efforts might be more effectually , directed tithe moral and social education of tlie pmple around them, and that Co-operative societies everywhere would become centres, not only of material help, but of ! intellectual culture and intelligent public spirit (Applause.)

The present annual cost of administration in the county, including he police, amountisl to abiut £110,900, and to meet this it would be necessary to levy rates to the extent of over 7d. in the £ but for the fact that the rates were assisted by an annual pay- ment of £15,000 from the River Wimver Navigation, , about £14,000 from the Government m half cost of pay ! and clothing of the police, £lO,OOO front Government towards main mots, and about £14,000 Men other grants, fines and fees, rents, he., which reduced the amount to be raised by rates (county police and hundred bridge rates) to ' about £58,000 per annum, requiring rates ht the amount of about aid. in the £ on the present ratable values, viz., ratable value for county rate £3,139,304 : ratable value for police rates, £2,759,823 ; and this cost also met an extraonlittary annual payment now made by the county to the Public Works Loan office of £14,221 1.55. on account of the Cattle Plague Loan in 1866, hut which expires in 1896. has often obtained a word of praise from as whilst it has been in progress; and now that it is issued in a com- plete form, after nearly 17 years' labour, Messrs. Cavell and Co., are to be warmly congratulated on the sure,. they Inv° achieved. It is almost a matter of courm ,no of every itsm dictionary that is issued that it in a.p aifvasrreupon its work Ia lust the rdeve,lo7.a,lsnd flirt name emplien, is something more than a dictionary ; and it is so I exhaustive in every respect—the outcome of so much thorough and original ressorch--that it has left all other I lexicons a hog, long way in the rear. The Impenal Dictionary, which has hitherto held the premier position, rWatan. m 2,922 pages, as ainst the 1,538 pages of ehster's Unabridged ; but'the Encyolopedic Dictionary extends to 5,829 pages. It sms originally intended to complete the work in twelve divisional volunes ; but the editor, Dr. Hunter, provided to much material that was good that it was finally decided to extend it to the fourteen volumes in which it is now offered to the public. As editor 1/r. Hunter has had the assistance of some if the chief scientific specialists in the country— from Professor Huxley downwards. Btyond this, I" presidents, secretaries, and members of scientific and learned neittim, the chief officers of religious bodies, University Profirtsors, Omen:anent officials, and a host I of private persons have rendered willing help by afford- ing information in many cases possessed by th-ennelves alone. The work has been brought as fa.r as possible up to date, words which have only just come into use being duly inserted in their places: and special atten- tion has been given to the insertion of American woods arid phrases which have not previously found a place in nay English dictionaries." Giving the neaning of a wont often means a chapter of history. For instance in treating of pyramid, we have a concise amount of the pyrainids of Egypt. and then a description of the game of billiards known as pyramids. And to with the latest discoveries in science; the student is helped at every turn, special cans being taken to include all technical terins—whether as relating to science, art, handierafts,'or sport. There is too, " a nearly exhaus- tive list of obsolete words from about Chaucer's time to the present, and, in addition, a complete vocabulary of words to be found in Scott and limns, the most extensively read authors ill Scottish literature." Col- loqualisms are inserted even when—a; they sometimes do—they merge into slang. This inay be objected h. by some, hoist seems tons that it is the moll course to take In a work which claims to be the met exhaustive dictionary of the English language yet iSSUIki. The spoken language of to-day—slangy as some of it may St—often becomes the written language-of to-morrow ; and it is surely better to include words atiout which readers care little than slut off sone ash, which students —for one purpose or another— may wish to know eve/VI/it/B. "Quotations illustrative of every sense of each word are given freely, and with mfull references as it was possible to give. In this rispoct the Encyclo- pudic Dictionary far surpasses all its predecesson, inasmuch earn them, with very few exceptions, only the name of an author is given, reference being ran-1y made to the name the work quoted from, and s ill m,int rarely to the page, chapter, or line of the work:' These quotations are the finest feature of the 'work. They add to the interest whilst they add to knowledge ; they make the dictionary in fact a readable book. With regard to pronunciation, the best is done that can be done. The mmt approved form is given first ; but other forms are added, and, as there is no standanl in such a matter, there is rean often for the exercise oh' choice. "In the earill of words ,dsrived directly front proper names, a brief account Iv. person in question is given either in the etemobigical portion of the article or in the definition. 'nine., brief account of Arirts is given in the article Arian, A." It should be added that the dictionary is illu.strated wherever illustnition is deemed necensary to aid textual explartition. Another !good feature is that every word described is priotel in bold, clear type, as that there is none of that painful seash as inevitable with closely printed, small tyre dictionaries. Iteganling the work-ass whole, we mnslo, speak too highly of it. It ion colmsal skill, learning, industry, and onterprise.

div.p: MR. BARI AT PRKSTON BROOK.

On Monday evening a crowded +fleeting was held at Preston Meek, in rapport of the candidature for the Daresbury Division of Mr. William It. Karp, who met with a very gratifying reception. The chair was occu- pied by Captain George Roger, and amongst those ulno, present, in addition to the emdidate, were the Rev. W. Fielding and Messrs. lI.J. hongton (Warrington). Luke: Jones, Benjamin Haddock, Alfresi Broom, F. Weir. Jos. ' Spruce. W. Pecenett, T. P. Taylor, Webb, John Jonas, kc. The Caseeetede, in opening the meeting, observed that Mr. Dreenall, one of the candidates, had been for a long : time a justice of the peace. He was no doubt an excel-: lent man, but penple who held positions for a lengce•ned : period were apt to get into a greove. It was inadvisablel to have a large proportion of magistrate+ in the County Councils. Ile considered it would be for better to put forwent and elect candidate, who were not magistrate.. , With respect to Mr. Linakor. he won a man who had an 1111111011,e amount of work 011 hi, Diode, and it seemed to him (the Chairman) that they should +int represents- I fives who were comparatively 'free, and who could give almost the whole of their ntiention Collie affairs of the ' electors. Seeing that Mr. Linaker was so much engrossed in bu.sines, he could hardly be expected to I do as well for them a.s Mr. Karp might he expected I to do. (Applause.) Mr. Es., in the course of a very able address. said that he believed that, nicer the passing of the Peony Post Act, no Art that bad been paeeed had been of such a good, practical nature as the Local Government Act, I IBM (Hear, hear.) The Act certainly was capable of I being worked for the good of the public, and he was sure I that it would very sonn make the public feel its hence% ' if it only got adininistered in a proper spirit. (Hear, hear.) It bestowed more benefit on the public than any Act Sill, the Penny Post Act, and none could doubt for a moment the enormous benefits of that Act. (Hear, heart Before that Art was ImAird a letter would cost mere than a man could earn for a day's work,if the letter had to go any great distanee. That Act met with a lot of opposition, and so did this. Since he made his first speech, a good deal of information had been given res- pecting the duties of the County Council. both from the platform and in the public prints. But he would elate a couple of incidents that had occurred in that Union, which might form an 1,111. for saying a few words more on this matter. One if thus' incidents occurred in the Appleton Divisionoshere a inan went canvassing a woman to vote for Mr. Joseph Knowles The woman kept pigs, and ehe asked the canvasser cent all this voting was about He replied "Well, they tell me that it is to do away with all the bother you have had in moving your pegs about, and if you rote for Joseph Knowles he is going Lod° away with all that." (Laugh- ter.) he," said she, then I shall vote for Mr. Knowles, for I have had noend of trouble with my pigs." (Renewed laughter.) The other incident occurred in tliatdivisinn,ceinewliere near Rocksavage. Two work- ingmen on seeing eime addresses posted were talking the matter over, when one ventured to ask what it was all for. Well," Raid the other, "they tell me there is a chap named Gnenall who bad a good job for twenty- five rears, and that there is a chap named Linalcer trying to do him out of it. (Laughter.) Now that is not fair, is it ?" "No," said the other, it isn't; but

did you ever known chop who had a good job but what there vras always somebody trying to do lihn out of it E' (Loud laughter.) After these two incidents he did not think a little more information on the matter would do any harm, and he proposed to read from an eminent work on the Act some of the chief duties that would devolve on the County Council. The two eminent barristers who were ihe authors of the work began by saying that the Art had two words stanmed upon it, viz., represmtation and derentralisation. If they now a photograph of mountain scenery they would call it a representation of mountain scenery, or the photograph of one's self was the n.presentation st alien self. The more it was like! the original, the better the representation was. And the • more their representative was like them in the County Council, the better they would be npresented. (Applause.) Decentralization means the act of distribu- ting among a number of places throughout the county the management cif its internal affairs, instead of work- ing them from one common centre, such as London. Lawyers and others would tell them that there is a great waste of time, and after all very unsatisfactory results, in haying to refer all 'natters to London, simply because the people in London know nothing about the matter that is referred to them. After having referred at some length Is the provisions of the'new Act,Mr. Karp said that if magistrates were to be elected on the County Councils the Act might as well never have been passed, for its object was to take power from the magistrates and give it to the rate- payers (Appian.) He did not think that the ratepayers would elect multstrates if they fairly understood the position. As regarded the management of the police, he thought Chit it ShOilld be solely in the hand.s of the public. The magistrates had also had power over the rating of roads. Soule of then' now said they would • relieve this, that, and the other. Why had they not I done it before' They had had the power—more power I than they would ever have again. He wished • to my a 'few words in regard to misrepresentations • in recent speeches of Mr. Linaker. In one of lot speeches Mr. Linaker mid, in reply to a questlon front I Mr. Gouge Percival, '• The only offices on the County • Council would be the clerk of the peace, the county bridgemaster and surveyor, the county treasurer, and • the county analyst " These were the only salaries he I would wish the.. understand would be paid out of the county rate. If In- had evainined the Act more care- fully., he would have fiiund that the clerk of the peace would not be paid out of the county rate; neither would , the justices' clerk. Did he mean to tell them that the whole administration of the reality was worked by three then? Another misrepresentation he made was on the ' matter of he assessment of the Manchester Ship Canal's property at Runcorn. He (Mr. Karp) admired his shrewdness in this matter, if there was nothing else to admire. It was well-known that Mr. Linaker and his family boils pre.ty big bill to come in as soon as the election was over. Ile was told it would be over £2,000, and with a bill of this kind ready to administer to the ratepayers the moment the election was over, who could wonder that he refused to disclose it before tile election takes place, or who could wonder at his futile attempt to glom over the case which had led to this large bill of costs. (Laughter.) Now did they want mpreienting or misrepresenting ? Ile would ask thein to vote for a candidate who would be likely to really npresent and to vote for their interests, and if by so doing their choice happened. fall on him he woUld do his best for the welfare of all. (Loud applause.) Mr. WY. IVOIMAI.I. inquired whether it was comet that Mr. Karp bad enterml into an agreement with Mr. Greenall to conic forward in order that the voting, being split between himself and Mr. Linaker, Mr. Dreenall would secure a majority, and no be elected. 'Laugh- ter.) Mr. EA.' characterised the statmnent as a ridiculous invention, and said lie had never in his life spoken to Mr. tireenall. (Applause.) Richanl Earp to be a lit and proper person to repremnt the Daresbury division in the Cheshire County Connell, and pledges itself to OM every effort to secure his return." (Applause.) Mr. BRN.I.IN HADLIOCIC seconded, and said lie did no because Mr. Karp was one of themselves; he was a resident amongst them, an employer of labour, and a ratepayer in the district. A grave respotnibifity rested upon the electors, and it behoved them to send to the Connell a representative full of energy, seal, and, above all, independence. (Applause.) Mr. Karp possessed off thine qualities, and he, therefore, asked them to support !Moto the utmost of their ability. (Applause.) Mr. H. J. lANIVrON, speaking in support (if the resolution, mid he was certain in his own mind that Mr. . .

Carp was a representative of the people. After having 550 years of experience of magisterial control of the ratepayers' motley. the people who found the money were now considered to sufficiently intelligent to be able to supervise its expenditure. The candidate in WhOge behalf that meeting was being hell was one who would never let an injustice be dune Dimly village in the Daresbury or any other division, and he was in every respect a fit and proper candidate. Ile had but little doubt onto what the result of the contest would be, but he urged them to Me every endeavour to place Mr. Eani at tho head of the poll on the day of election. (Applause.) div.head: PADGATE WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL.
div.p: PADGATE WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL.

The annual tea meeting in connection with the Wesleyan School, Padgate, was held on Tuesday evening. There was a very good attendance about 1.50 sitting down to tea. The ladies and gentlemen I who gave trays were : • Mesdames Thomas Bennett, William Bennett, John Smith, William Smith, Yates, Houghton, Harris, Richardson, White, Thos. Yates, Brindle, London, W. Thornton, Royston ; Messrs. Fowler Jenkins, and Henry Thornton.
Aft, tea azi entertainment was givgn, the Rev. G. E. Young presiding. Amongst others present were Rm.", W. Iliannett, E. Richardson, F. Wright, E. Ford, W. Y. Lawton, and W. (Reeve.

Mr. J. White, secretary of the School, submitted his I report. He was pleased to report that the work of the school during the past year had been very satisfactory. The number of scholars had now increased to 140, and the attendance had been much tatter, the average attendance being 40 lays and 20 girls in tile morning, and 54 boys and 40 girls in the afternoon. In 1887 the I total attendance was 55 in the morning and 71 in the I I afternoon. The number of teachers on the books is 18. I being two more than last year. The average attendance lad bast Bin the morningand 11 in the afternoon. Thu ' officers for the present par were as follows :—Superiffi tendents, Was.. F. Wright and H. Ward ; auditor, Mr. A. Be .nett librarian, Mr. T. S. Steel ; saving club secretary, Mr. J. F. White. The School Committee were Messrs. W. Bennett, James Ford, E. Richardson, T. Hughes, J. Taylor, and H. E. lb.collar. The total receipts for the year were £l3 Bs. 3d. ; the expenditure, £1355., leaving a balance in band of 3s. 3d. There were now 188 volumes in the seffial library but lie was sorry to say there bad been avery poor circulation during the year. The library had, however, been made free to the scholars, and in consequence they expected MOM would avail themselves of its privileges. The Band of Hope, chiefly owing to the efforts of Mr. E. Harris, Mr. Ward, and other [ateliers, was now in a Yin flourishing etiViti.e.m. (Applause.) ' " •

Society was pawing through very great changes, and they did not know what would be seen 20 or 30 years hence, but there would be great changes in the method of work as well as in scientific matters. It was wonderful what great stridm had , been made during the past 50 years, and since the time when the first locomotive engine was started in the ! month of October. 1827. RUNCORN PUBLIC HAW

Sir.—llefore granting a licence to the Theatre, our Magistrates rightly requirethatample means for emit are inaititaitsxl. Why shoithl net the name care be exercised with runpect to Runcorn Public Hall ? Ought not the people going them lo bean well safe-guarded as Theatre gores? On leaving that Hall on Wednesday night three streams of the audience, namely from the gallery, the body, and the reserve seats, met in one vestibule toga out by the smallest of the two doorways down a step into a dark street. The large doorway where there is plenty of space and lamp for the lighting was closed and in darknews. This is surely not as it ought to be.—Yours truly,

div.head: LOVER OF SAFETY
div.p: LOVER OF SAFETY
WARRINGTONIANS IN AMERICA.-ANOTHER INTERESTING LEITER.

..... Sir,—You have asked me to give you a few personal details of Mr. Winstanlev's life, since his arrival in the far west. Well, sir, I will do what I ran in compliance with your request. but! am afraid I shall not be able to tell you anything if a very exciting nature. Although lie has tovellisl so far-7,000 miles—by sea and land, through 1111.101 that was novel and fascinating, across prairi. Ouse nulling expanse streteliod out for hundreds of miles, skirting the tideless shores of great inland seas, through almost interminable birests, and over mountains on whose lofty woks reposed perpetual snow and whim, rugged sides were the chosen haunts of the grizzly bear —though he has passed through scenes as wonderful as those that Alice saw in Wonderland—yet, his travels have been singularly devoid of 'aiming incidents. No ; though he has probably travelled as far, and through scenes as strange. SA the Moor of Venice, yet, unlike Othello, be spealo not of Mon disastrous chime.. olmoiimivaeei.tentw by St... Land field, tut iukirlurcuudth (ii tiring being taken In the insolent foe?' Nay,he has not even... had his hair lifted" by the yell- ing Red-skins—those gentle denizens of the "Wild West." And since he has settled down in Salem, he has fired very quiet ly, and worked very hard. I.ike the rude fore-fathers of Gray's" Elegy." c Along tlue cool ..equestered vale of life He's pc.sed the even tenor or his way.- Mr. Winstmley has now been settled in his new home ler six months. In the many letters he lia.s written to me he has frequently spoken of the pleasing beauties of the home of his ndoption. The softness of theclimate, and the romantic grandeurof the scenery, the marvellous fertility of the soil, and the prodigious sizeand excellence of the fruits and vegetables, have alike excited his wonder and admiration. He has found many, and warm friusols, and kIA been the recipient of many kind- nesses at their hands. It has been a common occurrence or his friends to drive Idin and his wife :hoot the country, and to make them pimento of bags and basket of delicious fruits—such as would raise the envy of a duke's head gardener. Amongst their many kind friends are the minister and his wife—Mr. and Mrs. Sewall. Mr. I Vrinstanlev has at different times expressed his grati- tude for the unfailing kindness of this Indy and gentle. man. It stvins that out West the ministers practice medicine on well as preach the IRospel. and these kind AOlliS have prescrilml for Mr. Winstanlev who has occa. sionally been ailing a little—baring got a cold on his passage out and not having become acclimatized no readily as his family—who are all enjoying splendid healtE.

thud a letter the other day from Mrs. Mlnstanley I who thus speaks of Mrs. Newtll—" To my mind she is like an angel in disguise. Yon may possibly laugh at me, hut without excretion she is the truest model of a Christian I ever met with in my life. She haa been a true friend to us all ; she is like a sister to Me, and is ever anxious both for our spiritual and temporal wel- fare." Notwithstanding all the kindness of their new friends, however, thy cannot forget the old friends they left behind them in Warrington. " Give me my old friends," writes Mrs. Winstanley. "There are no faces to me like the old faces. Every day I long to see some dear old fare or other, but no old fare appears." Yet they are very happy indeed, and would not on any account, like to 001110 track to Warrinton. Mr. Winstanley bought a farm and house immediately on his arrival in' Salem. His son drives him to town every mornmgAnd drives him home again in the evening. Ile describes Dale drives as very charming. The clear- ness of the atmosphere is surprising. Mount Hood, with its snow-cappod peak, is clearly discernible, though distant 80 miles. Mr. Winstanley--as many of your reader, know, is a joiner—and has had constant employ- ment up till Derember Ist, at good wages, namely, 18 dollars a week. equal in our money to about RS 155. He says that load is very cheap, and, ache lives in his own house, and took an abundant supply of clothing with hint, he inns very little expense His children are intensely pleased with their new life and new surroundings. His son, a lad of 15, is so fasci- nated with everything ahmt them, that he simply revels in it all, his days being spent in riding, shooting, fishing E.., to his heart's content. Mr. Winstanley has again and aein thanked me for the "Examiner," which I send lum regularly. He says he likes it better than any paper I send him, and as for the papers out there, he doesn't care much about them. So you see, Mr. Editor, you will have to mind your P's and Q's and keep I the" Examiner" up to the mark, for he shows the paper to his friends out there, anti tells them, "There, that's the sort of paper for you ; that's how we do things in Warrington." Y.tt will be pleased to hear that I had a letter front Mr. Porter yesterday. He and his family are in capital health. He says," Later on I will send yOll a letter for publication in accordance with my promise to Mr. Walker, giving an account of my travels. I have been through every State it America, and overy province in Canatli, and an doubt nty letter will he of interest to .cone of the readers of tile" F.xaminer." And now, Mr. Editor, twill close—Yours
JOAN GANDY 23 Chttrelpatreet, Warrington.
THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL. RUNCORN. . . . .

If ant person acquain-tiri-rrii.No Man's Land and its I surroundings were now admitted within the high palings which now enclose the neighbourhood he would be ast bed at the great change effected in the aspect of the place lathe course of a few brief months. Castle Reek, where Ethelfleda's Castle stood, is fast disappear- ing before tile quarryman's tools, and daily the oceupants of the houses are startled by the sound of explosives blowing up the stone. Tlmough No Matis Land a deep excavation has been made, and the direction of the Ship Canal at this particular spot is admirably shown by the curved rutting of the navvies' spades. But the mast important work carried on is the forming of the river avail of the canal, and night and day, when the tide is out, ceaseless activity is displayed. Above the surface of the water 300 feet (tithe wall, which is about 25 feet wide at the bottom and about 18 feet wide at the top, can now be seen. This moresents an enormous weight of concrete and gravel, and to those who knew the difficulty of driving steel piles for the dams, an immense amount of labour. lathe construction of the wall, the stone from Castle Rock is extensively used. At one part the wall is ready for the coping stones. The con.strue. Con of the wall is in course of being extended still further towards Runcorn lint go. and for this purpose there is a dam 80 tees in length. It is at present filled with a hard muddy substance, which lots to be removed by hand labour, and the water is pumped out, when twesAary, by a steam pump tool on a boat, drawn alongside. Ins few weeks it is expected that the canal wall will reach from No Man's Land to Runcorn Bridge. Opposite the old ferry, wooden ales are being driven be ; steam power into the sand tusk. Forty feet in length the piles are driven into the bed of. the river a depth of 25 let, so so to firmly resist the action of the tide. The formation of the canal wall, iS noon to be commeneed at this spot. At the other end of the Eilction, under Mr. Gregsonss control, Randle's sluice is approaching com- pletion. and the diversion of the Latchtonl Canal is under way, while in a tear days the work of making, a tented to carry the pipes of the Liverpool Waterworks under the Ship Canal will he commenced. WARRINGTON AND NEIGHBOURHOOD.

Steady and continuous progress is being made on the whole length of the a.anal near Warrington. On or near bathe site of the intended Latchford locks three steam narvies are at work just now and the rutting is rapidly being widened to the full width of the lorks, the 'MX,oa of deepening the channel heing also mirried on. In this neighbourhood the work of laving the immolation of the intended emlmnkinent for tha:deviated Warringtion anal Altrineham railway is enntinued and much ad the spoil which iA constantly being emptied (nail the buckets of the dram navvim is utilised for this purprwe. Almost ,;alway to wean stoekton float, a n.ll.atrlif ,r,l nation ss, nsvvy al. os effective ~ rvie, in s.64lening the of the canal. The new road which is to run jint 'he upper reaches of Werh-laue and Common- areewee.,

lane, as ,MIP compensation for the closing of the latter In note pretty well advanced. Work also continues advance in the neighbourhood of Lower Walton and Acton Grange, and on Arpley Meadows. ACCIDENTS. On Wednesd yen accident happened on the canal at Statham whereby a man named Chilton was somewhat injured about the face and head by falling down a well. Another man who, lives in Cockhoolge-lane, Warrington, has been received into the hospital at Thelwall suffering front concussion of the brain. This WrlA caused by his falling down the side of the cutting near Acton Grange, and alighting on his head. He iS progressing favour ably.

That as the day of election of County Councillors approaches, apathy is giving way to keen interest, ' and the absorbing theme at the present time is— " who will he. the successful candidates? "

That to all intents and purposes the contests are non-political. The ratepayem are asked to vote not so much upon measures as men, and in arriving at a decision as to who shall have their support, they can only consider which candidate from his personal character and ability, and his past career, is most likely to protect the interests of the people, and enlarge the bounds of their freedom in the future May the best men win. That Mr. W. 11. Linaker will address a meeting of his supporters, in the l'ublic Hall, Runcorn, (this) Sat tirday evening, commencing at seven o'clock. That, although the 'sudden death of the half- day holiday " in Runcorn is announced in a black bordered placard, a large number of the tradesmen's places of business were closed on Thursday ; but there is no disguising the fact that "geese-eyed jealousy is gradually causing the movement to be broken up. In Widnes the half-day holiday is an institution that has stood the test of years, and is much prieed by both tradesmen and assistants, and it is not to the credit o: Runcorn shopkeepers that they cannot keep &similar organisation in existence! for °Venn few months.

--TiketiWeinid;;Tii; town could be as easily and as advantageously carried on in five days and a half as in six days, and the turnover would be none the less. Surely Runcorn is not to be behind Wid- nes in a matter of this kind.

That the members of the Musical Society made a highly successful first appearance before the Wine lon Tuesday evening, and it is hoped that the Society is established on a firm and enduring ' foundation. It ion pity the working classes were not bettor represented amongst the audience, but perhaps "music's golden tongue " will woo more listeners on the next occasion. although the num- her present on Tuesday was by no means meagre. That Mr. E. K. Muspratt has been elevated to the aldermanic Bench on the Lancashire County Coun- cil, for the term of three years; and it will now be necessary to elect another councillor front Widnes Division.

div.head: -SIR WALTER RALEIGH AND HIS TIMES."
div.p: -SIR WALTER RALEIGH AND HIS TIMES."

In Runcorn Public Hall, on Wednesday evening, the Rev. J. W. Dawson, of Glasgow, delivered his , popular lecture "Sir Walter Raleigh and his times" to a large audience. The proceeds of the lecture am to he devoted to the Camden Trust Fund. Mr. John Simpson occupied the chair. He was sup- I ported on the platform, besides the lecturer, by the Revs. 11. Burson, McKendrew, A. Burnett, and J. , Judson, and Messrs. S. C. Beckett, C. Littler, Garri- son, T. Boote, G. Yarwood, Rawlinson, T. Simister, G. Bellamy, P. Speakman, R. Norman, Unsworth, and F. 3.:Sorman. The Lecturer gave a rapid and vivid sketch of the England of Elizabeth, alluding to its seamen —Drake, Frobisher, and Gilbert—its statesmen, such as Burleigh, and amongst its poets, Shakespeare and ISpenser. The greatness of the time, he said, was proved by the men who lived in it. Great times produced great men, and small times gave Us small men. With regard to Raleigh they were struck by his versatility, for he could do most things better than most men. There was no end to his versatility, and it really seemed to some that he had within himself the whole spirit of the Elizabethan age, and he (the Lecturer) ventured to speak of him as the last great hero of a great period. (Applause.) The Lecturer described in glowing language the early years of Raleigh, his rise at Court, and the part he took in the destruction of the Spanish Armada. Passing on to recount the imprisonment of Raleigh under James, it was then, the Lecturer remarked, that lie began to writes book," The History of the World," which would live when the memory of Jame: had died in the bottomless ocean of infamous oblivion. Many noble books 111,1 been written in prison, but this was one of the grandest and noblest. It was a book which had influenced the lives of four of the noblest men who ever lived .John Elliott, John Hampden, John Milton, and Oliver Cromwell. If anyone asked what was the secret of the great- ness of Elizabeth's age, he would my that it was the protound belief in God which dominated the men of that age. (Applause.) Those men believed in God, and lived ea though they did. Humphrey Gilbert once wrote to the Secretary of State that he was detained by a South-west wind of God's sending. Let them imagine what would be thought if a sea captain wrote to a Secretary of State in that way to-day. (Laughter.) Raleigh's disastrous voyage in march of Eldorado, his return to the tower, and, finally, his execution, were, together with many other incidents of his eventful life, enlarged upon in eloquent language by the Lecturer. The lecture throughout was of the deepest interest, and the applause was frequent and hearty. Mr. F. J. Norman proposed a vote of thanks to the lecturer, which was seconded by Mr. Timothy Simister, and carried unanimously. After a similar compliment had been paid to the Chairman for presiding, the meeting was dispersed by the pronunciation of the Benediction.

div.head: COUNTY COUNCILS. FIRST MEETING.
div.p: THE COUNTY COUNCILS. FIRST MEETING.

The Lancashire County Council met on Thursday at the County Ilall,Preston,as a Provisional Council, to discharge certain duties imposed upon them by , Act of Parliament prior to their taking over from I the magistrates the general administrative work of the county. All members presented themselves with the except'n of two-- Mr. Arthur Appleby (Ilyndbum)and Mr. John Iludson(Brierclilfe),--and made the declaration prescribed by the statute. The Right Don J. T. Llibbert, who for many years has discharged the duties of Vice Chairman of the Court of Annual Session under Lord Derby's Chair- manship, was unanimously appointed chairman for this and any subsequent provisional meet- ings of the Council. Mr. Ilibbert acknowledged the honour done to him, and expressed a hope that the members of the new Council would bring to bear in their communications those habits of courtesy, fairness, and gentlemanly dealing; which would tend to place this County Council of the County Palatine of Lancaster in the front rank of such administrative bodies. The next important business was the election of 35 aldermen. This delicate work, though it occupied a good time, was accomplished very amicably. It was agreed by the Council in the first place, not to go outside its own ranks; and. next, that two aldermen should be selectee from the representatives of the Lancaster Quarter Sessional district, nine from those of Preston, 111 from those of West Derby, and 13 from the repro- I sentatives of the Salford Hundred. Thirty-five aldermen were chosen from the newly elected body, , so that there will now be that number of vacancies to till up between this and the 14th of February. Eighteen of the 33 aldermen will retire at the end of three years. The meeting, which began at noon, did not terminate until seven in the evening.
