RI•NCORN.-NOIITH DIVISION. MAJOR HAZLEHURST'S MEETING.

_ .... Major C. IV. liaslehurst, one of the candidates for the , North Division of Runcorn, addressed a Imeting of the , electors in the Forester's Hall, Runcorn, on Thursday evening. The chair was occupied by the Rev. W. Fres- ton, and ainetert the gentlemen on the platform, in nddion to the candidate, were Messrs. W. I). Jolliffe, J. R. Frith' and J. Meadowcmft. There woos favour- -1 I able attendance of voters.

The CHAIRMAN, in the iinurse of his introductory remarks, explained that Mr. Wigg, who had been expeo- • ted to preside. WAS unable to do so, and went on to say that the contest in which they were engaged vies not being fought on political grounds. That meting was essentially a non-political one. They were there to din- cuts the merits of their candidate, who, he thought, stood Mei,' well in his shoes. (A Voice : °Ws a tidy lump," I and laughter.) Their candidate also stood very well in popular favour—(cheers)—and he could safely say that I they intended to elect him. Be regret I that Mr. Brundrit, who had I iert mainly instrumental in securing I two members for Runcorn, had not been able to come forward as their candidate. Mr. Brundrit, however, was disqualified, and he maintained that Mr. Haslehurst, as a Runenrn man, was the candidate, par eardlew, who should be elected to represent that division of noncom. (Cheers.)

The eIIiTIOATE, Who WAS heartily cheered on rising 'to addrees the meeting, briefly returned thanks for the cordial nature of his reception. The tickets on which he was seeking the suffragen of the electors of the division were, he said, the tickets of economy and efficiency. As a matter of fact, he thought that economy would have 'to he used, but he considered that, while spending money in an economical manner, they must pay due regard to seeing that it WWI spent efficiently. (Clteers.) They wore continually approached with the idea that he was coming out sea political candidate. That idea he controverted, for, he said he could assure them that from the very start it was his intention net to come out as such, andhe had not yet altered that intention. He was ab.lutely a non-political candidate. If the contest had been one of politi., almost the first thing done would have been to make Same arrangement Well the political parties, but he had never had even a cony.- I nation with either party. A great deal was (Aid to the effect that magistrates should not offer thernselv. as ; county council candidates. Cnfortunately, he was in the position of being a magistrate, but he could not . help that. He WIA appointed some eight years ago, before County Councils were talked nI. His contention was that, having been nominated by the ratepayers, he came out on similar lines to anyone elne nominatail by the ratepayers. If, at the tinny that the Bill was framed, it had been intended that magistrates should not reale forward as candidates, there Weald have been a en,.,. . .

doing so. Failing that, they had a perfect right to offer themselves for election, anti, I RO far as he saw, there was no sin in boing a magistnite. (Cheers.) The magisterial body had had county work in hand for 582 years, and the fart that no strong . . . .

agitation had ever arisen against their mode of atiminis- : teethes was sufficient to show that they had nor done anything very wrong. Up to the commencement of the working of the festal tiovernment Act magietrates had had control of the judicial, administrative, and financial . parts of county affairs, but most of the work they had hitherto performed would he taken over by tile new : Councils. Flaying read a list of the duties that would devolve upon the new bodies, Mr. Hulehurst said that members of the County Councils would have to look forward to a very great deal of work, and it would take a long time before they got into proper working order. With reference to the administration of the magi-Ur-atm, he might tell them that there was a pretty universal opinion among men who knew a great deal about the work of magisvates, that it had been very well carried out. Fapecially SO had it been in the county of Chester, whirls, with the one exeeption of Somers+esishy WILA the lowest rated etionty in England. Having quote:l at some length figures regarding the financial administration of the county, taken from a statement Hated by the county auditor, Mr. Harlehurst mid that it was made evident that tbe county rate would have to be increased by one penny lathe pound, and it would be the duty of the Council, after it had got into working order, to see in what way the rate could be reduced, consistent with efficiency. (Cheers.) One great question at the present time mm—where should the meetings of the new Council beheld. There was ample accommodation at Chester and Knutsford, and it would Ise his endeavour to keep the work schere it had been transacted before, simply because those places, having during the last ten years had large sums of money spent upon them, were, so regarshel room and proper accommodation, ready for the UFO of the County Council. It would therefore, in his opinion, be unnecessary to incur expenditure its going anywhere (Chem.) Mr. .1. MEADOWCNOFT proposed "That in the opinion of this meeting Mr. Charles Whiteway Hatleisurst Li a fit and proper person to represent Runeorn North Division in the Cheshire County Council. and that this sleeting pledges itself to use all the legitimate means in its mower to secure Mr. HarlehursCs return on Tuesday next by a large majority." (Cheers.) There was, Mr. Meadow. croft said, an old saying "that good wine needed no bush," and he was equally sure that the resolution he had proposed needed lla commendation from him to ensure it a hearty welcome at the hand.s of these present. The speeell that had been given by Mr. Ilaxlehurst showed that he had a clear and intelligent conception of the Act relating to the County Councils. As the head of an important industry in the town, Mr. Flulehurst 'sad a claim upon the working classes of Runcorn from a rate- payer's trent of view. The firm whieh he represented had for a long time provided wages and sustenance for a eonsiderable number of workingmen. Mr. Harle. burst's commercial experience would serve 111111 in good stead its the consideration of financial matters. He believed that Mr. flarlehurst was the best eandidatethat they coold have, but he wished to remind them that, in order to secure his mt.!, it would be necessary that some work should be done. They must vigorously push forwent his candidatnre, in order to show their appns . elation by snaking Isis victory as overwhelming as I possible Mr. INITP, in seconding the propositioureferred to the , ' long connection of the Harleburd family with Runcorn, ' and to that family he attributed Much of the prosperity

A meeting in support of the candidature of Mr, W. Linaker was held last night, in the Foresters Hall, Devonshie. Span'. There was a fair attendance, and Dr. Robituon occupied the chair. Mr. LINAHMI, after a few preliminary remarks, said so far as he and Mr. Ilaglehurst were concerned, the election would be fought upon perfectly friendly grounds. (Hoar, hear.) He objected to the candidature of Mr. Hatlelmrst for two reasons—firstly because he was a justice of the peace for the county, and secondly lrnoaaoe he had no knowledge of the public busineos of the iinportant town ot Runcorn or of county matters. The County Council together with certain justices would have control of the police, but he (Mr. Linaker) did not consider it equitable that men who utt in judgment upon offences eamnittel by the public generally, should have any control whatever over the police. If the ratepayers thought tit to return two magistrates from Runcorn, well mu gm'. but he had come forward •0 a protest against a return to the old system. (Ap- plause.) Mr. Ilaxlehurst said if he were returned, he would, as a large ratepayer, naturally see to the economical expenditure of the county monies. The county rate was about 4.d. or 4fd. in the £, and was paid by the Guardians of the seveml unions. MagettratN web o esrojrcie members of the Board of Guardians,but not a single magistrate attended the in,s.tings at Dutton of the Board of Guardians. They entirely neglected to are to the expenditure of a rate of 2s. to 2.4 &lout of which that 4 came (Applause.) —ln reply lan question handed up to him Mr. Linaker said he was of opinion that all licensing business in the first instance should be in the hands of the local authority, which at the present time would mean the Local Board of Commissioners. and that there should be an appeal from such Board, not to the court if Quarter Sessions, but to the County Council (Applause). On the question of local option, he stated he WU in favour of Sunday closing. (Hear' hear.) As Mr. Ilatlehurat's supporters had introduced politics, he could only say he the speaker) was a Radical and supported Mr. Gladstone in his scheme for Home Rule to Ireland (Applause.) Hots was in the chair, and he geld, in intro- ducing the candidate, that it was time there should be a ' change in the administration of county affairs, as it is not possible for magistates, who two frequently arrange public business round their own private tables, toot in : the interests of the general body of ratepayers.—Mr. Ssetrox said he was sorry to have to allude to personal 'matters I fore Inc dealt with the aspects of the County ;Government Act. These personal attacks made by Mr. Lister on his (Mr. Stelfox's) private business occupied a good deal of time, and he was sorry he had to allude to them. He had thought that Mr. Litter's attack would I have been final, but heunderstood that at his meeting on Wednesday he returned to the attack He held that Mr. Lister had no right to interfere with his private business, and Mr. Lister must have employed clerks paid by the Treasury to go through the court . books for the purpose of ascertaining the quantity of cases he passed through court. He had stated that he passed 2,000 cases, and he found on examination that the exact number was 1.700 last year, but the year before the number was 2,500, so that the average was upwards of the number stated. He also stated that he paid £l5O as fees: if he had gime into lour figures he would have been nearer the mark. As to the amount of rates he paid, Mr. Lister had the assistant.overseer at his meeting to show that he only paid Ltl La. 2d. in rates and taxes. He produced his receipts, and asked if any- one wished to examine them as they were there. He did not add the shillings whorl he totalled the amount, or the sums would have exceeded £3s—Sir. div.head: PARR'S BANKING COMPANY.
div.p: PARR'S BANKING COMPANY.
ANNUAL MEETING.

The annual ordinary meeting 01 the directors and shareholders of this Company was held at the Bank Premises, Winwick.st., Warrington, yesterday at noonfor the purpose of receiving the annual report, and for the transaction of other yearly business. , Mr. J. Charlton Parr presided, and there was a good attendance of shareholders.

131.CTORS' REPORT. , The following report of the directors was submitted : "The Directors in submitting to the shareholders the annual balanee sheet, certified by the auditor. have to , report that the position and prospects of the business ' continue to ill, in every way satisfactory. Including ' £18,418 19s. Bd. brought (nen previous account, the net balanneof profits. after Providing amply for all bad and doubtful debts, and rebating the current bills at five per cent., is £124.912 fn. 11d. The distribution of this sum, recommended liv the Directors, is as follows :—lnterim half-yearlydivitlend. at 15 per cent. per annum, declared 27th July. £45,000 Os. DI. ; dividend to be now paki at the rate of 15 per cent. per annum, free of income tax, £42,000 Os. Ott. ; bonus of 10, per share, free of income tax, £14,000 00. Ckl. ; to property account, £502700. Pd.; Ixdarge to next amount, £21,912 to. 11. ; total, £124,912 Os. 11d. The Directors WllO retire at this time by rotation an:Mr. Thomas 11. Dixon. Mr. Alfred Turner, Mr. Henry Warren Meade-King, Mr. C. F. Parr, and Mr. Thomas I'. Parr, all of whom ant eligible and an, recom- mended for re-election." The Chairman, in pro/swing the adoption of the report, congratulated the share- holders on the encouraging features of the balance sheet. The figures werethe largest they had yet had the pleasure of presenting, and the relative amount ttf the net profit might be taken 3.4 evident" that the bitsint"s had been carefully and successfully conducted. There had been a steady increase in the business, which had not only enabled them to maintain their dividends and profits during the long period of unexampled depression, but whieli should on the revival of trade afford them a some- what larger earning capacity when energy should have taken the place of inactivity and despondency. With the keen competition that now existed amongst Isinks, it could not be expected that the same profits would accrue to an anstssion of the business which they might have expected some years ego. Although they inust not jump bathe conelinitm that, because things win, somewhat brighter, there was a period of uninterrupted prosperity before them, still he thought they might venture to hope, judging the present by the light of the past, that the revival that was now in progress, though struggling and weak at the present.svas still apparent and tangible, that it would make satisfactory progress, and that it would be sound and lasting. Mr. Parr also alluded to the steady increase in the number of shareholders. They now numbered 1,000, he said, and by increas- ing responsible shareholders and so widening the basis on which the bank stood, they were introducing a larger share of the public to participate in their pros- , perity, and to assist in promoting the bank's interest. ' They might remember that at the period of the last ' annual meeting a. scheme was supposed to be in the mind cd the Chancellor of the Exchequer for the reduction of the interest on the National Debt. Mr. tionthen, aides' by the exceptional position of the money market, and the low ritre of interest that then mint, and assisted by the gmat linnet:try and financial powere of the country, I woo able to carry to a successful solution one of the , grog • sr hats, perhaps. ot sucressful manes' that this ettottiry had ever seen. whereby the interest on the Nationnl Debt was rethreed from 3 per cent. to 21 ner cent., and would be still further redueel to 21 in fifteen year's time, thereby relieving the taxpayer

Iron an immediate burden of a million and a quarter, with a still further relief in fifteen years' time of double that amount—two millions and a half. Front a selfish point of view some of them inight regret the interference with their time honoured consols, and deplore the violation of the sweet simplicity of the 3 per rents., but that mint not dim their appreciation of the capacity. boldniiiis, and ability with which the Chancellor of the Ftehequer had carried through his masterlyconeeption. Turning to the balance sheet, it would be seen that the items for capital and reserve fund were unchanged, and that the money lodged had been increased by £400,000. This might be partly due to temporary I,ircumstances, but ' it was a satisfactory figure, and one pleasant to eontem- plate. The value of the bank property stood at £lBO,OOO. The Chairman made further reference to the balance sheet, and concluded by proposing its adoption along with the report—The proposition was seconded by Mr. N. Eckersley. and carried unanimously. ovvvo eestit.ss•

On the motion of Mr. A. Turner, seconded by Mr. John White, it was resolved that a dividend and bonus as recommended by the directors la. paid.—Capttin Withington proposed, Mr. T. Paterson seconded, and ' it was resnlved, that the directors be thanked for their services, and that their remuneration for the ensuing year be £5,000. —The retiring directors were re-elected on the motion of Mr. J. Hutchings. seconded by the Rey. W. 11. Williams—Mr. J. C. Stead, accountant, Liver- pool, was, en the motion of Mr. C. Griffiths, wended by Mr. James Jolley, re-appointed auditor to the Com- pany. He briefly returned thanks.—Votes of thanks to the manager, the secretary, and the officers of the corn- pany, for their services during the past year, and to the Chairman for presiding, terminated the meeting.

The contest between members of the Warrington and Leicester Gymnasiums, in the first round of the contest for the Challenge Shield of the National Physical Recreation Society, took place at the Drill Hall, on Thursday evening, before a good audience. • Although the Leicester Gymnasium had been ! started a month before the establishment of the , Warrington institution, the result was most gratify- I lag to the promoters of the local institution, as well as to the bulk of the spectator, The Mayor (Alderman T. Warren, of the Warrington team, showed , particular skill, and his performance turned the scale and gained victory for his side. div.head: DISASTROUS EXPLOSION AT CREWE STEEL WORKS. TWENTY MEN INJURED. . .
div.p: DISASTROUS EXPLOSION AT CREWE STEEL WORKS. TWENTY MEN INJURED. . .

..... One of the most disastrous accidents that hag ever happened at Crewe occurred just before eight o'clock yesterday morning, at the extensive works of tlm Lon- don and North-Western Railway Company. The company make their own steel by what is known as the Bessemer process, and a large number of men arecon- stantly employed in the Bessemer pits. Just before eight 'o'clock the cupola,or ladle, was full oi molten metal,readE I to be poured into the ladle which contained about seven or eight tons of the boiling fluid, and it was being worked in position by machinery. When the spur gearing or cog wheels above gave way, the ladle was overturned, end the whole of the boiling metal was turned into the pit. It is supposed ;Bat the bottom of the pit was wet, for there followed a loud explosion, and the metal flew over the shop, scalding over twenty men, some very badly. The clothes of one or two were set on fire. but (hey were covered with clata and blankets by a little army of comrades who rushed to their rescue. Thirteen of the worst injured were taken to the London and North-Western Company's Hospital by a special train. The cause of the accident was a collapse of the spur gearing, the large wheel lying broken into half a down pieces ; every part where it has helices shows a clear and solid fracture. The officials declare the break- ing office wheel lobe inexplicable. PROSECUTION AND ESCAPE OF MR. W. O'BRIEN.— EXTRAORDINARY. RCENE.,_ . ,

A scene almost without parralel in recent Irish history occurred on Thursday, at Carrick-on-Suir. Mr. W. O'Brien, M.P., went down to that place to answer before two of the o removables " a charge of inciting the people to withhold vents lawfully due and to bnyoott land-grabbers." The police authri2ties had pro- claimed " the district, hut the people newel so assembled to the number of ten or twelve thousand, and gave Mr.O'Brienaveryenthusiasticreception. Thepolice, who were in full passemion of the town, prevented the people from approaching the Courthouse. Mr. O'Brien and Mr. T. Healey, M.P., his counsel, protested against this, and the police then made a brutal attack en the two hon. members. Mr. O'Brien was hustled and dragged about, and Mr. Healy was threatened with a baronet stab by a policeman. One. inside the court, boils the defendant and his counsel vigorously protested against the treatment they had received. In support of the charge the usual police evidence WAS given. At the close of the case for the prosecution, Mr. , Healy applied for witness summonses agishist Lord Salisbury nod Mr. Balfour, hut the Bench refused to grant the application. The deeision was! dimpproved of by the people, whereupon the Bench ordered the court to be cleared. Mr. O'Brien, and Mr. ' Healy rose, and said they would " clear out" also. The polkas endeavoured, hut in vain, to seize Mr. O'Brien and compel him to remain, and the hon. member eventually got outside the Courthouse. Here thousands of people formed a dense mass around him. The police charged again and again, but were likable to capture the hon. gentleman. The magistrates issued a warrant for his arrest. In the police charges a large number of people received baronet wounds. A Carrick-oreSuir correspondent says that Mr. Wm. O'Brien, NP.. was not captured up to last evening, although the police mere scouring the country in all directions. Soldiers wen. drafted into Carrick-on-Suir on Friday. The magistrates opened the Crimes Act Court at noon, and sentenced him in his absence to four months' imprisonment without hard labour. BAYONET CHARGE AT CLONAKILTY. " "'"

There was some stone- throwing amt several bayonet charges, and eleven I persona—six civilians and five policemen—are reported injured.
